chapters: The woman whom You gave me

events.text: Black. Then the garden at evening, very close among the leaves. A wind is coming through the trees from far off, bending them one after another in a long wave, like footsteps. Leaves shiver. Between dark leaves, a man's eye, wide and afraid (Adam, cast portrait): the same eye that opened on the first breath in The Garden.
The wind comes nearer, tree by tree, each wave louder, then stops. Total silence.

events.speaker: GOD
events.text: Where are you?
Silence on black.

Flash-forward montage, about one second a shot, a low boom on the first frame: a whirling sword of flame igniting in the eastern opening of the garden, huge; fruit torn from a branch; the serpent's eye, very close; fig leaves pulled from a branch; thorns breaking through cracked ground; a grain of dust; two small figures walking east into a dark land, the fire behind them. Then black.
Montage at full drive; the flame roars on the last shot, then the music cuts to nothing.
Where The Garden ended: the tree in the middle of the garden at dusk, perfectly still. Something moves in the long grass at its foot.

events.speaker: GUIDE
events.text: The last chapter ended with a man and a woman, naked and unashamed, in a very good world. This chapter answers the question every reader eventually asks. If the world began like that, why is it like this? It begins with a question. Not God's question. Another voice asks first.
THE FALL / Genesis 3:1 to 24
Title over the grass at the foot of the tree. A low hit, a dark swell, then quiet.

Low in the grass, very close: scales sliding past, the serpent moving through the garden toward its centre. Then the woman beneath the tree, seen from the shoulders up, turning toward a sound in the branches (Eve, cast portrait).

events.speaker: READER
events.text: Now the serpent was more crafty than any beast of the field that the LORD God had made. And he said to the woman, “Did God really say, ‘You must not eat from any tree in the garden?’”

events.speaker: GUIDE
events.text: The chapter opens with a pun English cannot keep. The pair were naked, arummim. The serpent is crafty, arum. The two words sound almost the same.

Egypt, remembered. A brick yard under a white sun, and above it on a palace wall a carved king wearing the rearing cobra on his brow, gold catching the light. Cut to the wilderness camp by day: the brick-maker, free now, sitting at his tent door, a scar on his forearm, looking at the dust.

events.speaker: GUIDE
events.text: The people who first heard this had just come out of Egypt, where a rearing cobra crowned Pharaoh's head. In that world the snake meant wisdom, healing, power. Genesis refuses to make it a god. It is a creature the LORD God had made, and it ends this chapter eating dust.

events.speaker: GUIDE
events.text: Later Scripture names the voice behind it:

events.speaker: READER
events.text: that ancient serpent called the devil and Satan

events.speaker: GUIDE
events.text: Jesus calls him

events.speaker: READER
events.text: the father of lies
The serpent's eye, very close. Silence.

events.speaker: GUIDE
events.text: And watch how he works. He never commands. He only asks. His first move is a question about what God said.
Under the tree, the serpent among the branches above her, a thin dark line against the leaves; she looks up at it, calm, unafraid.

events.speaker: READER
events.text: The woman answered the serpent, “We may eat the fruit of the trees of the garden,

events.speaker: READER
events.text: but about the fruit of the tree in the middle of the garden, God has said, ‘You must not eat of it or touch it, or you will die.’”

events.speaker: READER
events.text: “You will not surely die,” the serpent told the woman.

events.speaker: READER
events.text: “For God knows that in the day you eat of it, your eyes will be opened and you will be like God, knowing good and evil.”

On screen over the tree, the three versions one above the other. God's words, Genesis 2:16 to 17. Her words, with FREELY fading out, OR TOUCH IT appearing, and SURELY falling away. Then the serpent's, with NOT dropping in front of God's own words. A soft hit on each change.

events.speaker: GUIDE
events.text: Lay the two side by side and you can watch the lie being built. God said, eat freely from every tree, with one limit and a clear warning. She drops the freely, adds touching, and softens the warning. She shrinks the gift and enlarges the limit.

events.speaker: GUIDE
events.text: Then the serpent takes God's own words and puts a not in front of them. He contradicts God word for word, and he paints the Giver of every tree as jealous, holding something good back.
NOT settles on screen in front of God's words. One low hit.

events.speaker: GUIDE
events.text: Notice too that the narrator says the LORD God, His covenant name. In this conversation they say only God. The personal name drops out just as trust in Him is dissolving.

events.speaker: GUIDE
events.text: The root of sin, as Genesis tells it, is not ignorance. It is distrust. A willingness to believe that God is holding back something good, and that His word can be edited.
Hold on the fruit in the branches. One low tone.

Set piece: the eating. Extreme slow motion and close: the fruit hanging in warm light; her eyes on it; her hand rising through the leaves; fingers closing; the branch springing back as the fruit comes away, leaves falling. She turns and holds it out. His hand takes it (Adam, cast portrait). Fruit of no particular kind, never an apple.

events.speaker: READER
events.text: When the woman saw that the tree was good for food and pleasing to the eyes, and that it was desirable for obtaining wisdom, she took the fruit and ate it. She also gave some to her husband who was with her, and he ate it.

Set piece: the eating, no narration. A rising pulse under the slow motion; on the bite the score cuts out and there is only the wind. The warm light goes cold as a cloud crosses the garden; the wind turns; leaves fall.

Hard cut: an eye opening, very close, exactly as the man's eye opened on his first breath in The Garden, but now the eye is afraid. Then hands tearing broad fig leaves from a branch, fast, the leaves tied together with fibre.

events.speaker: READER
events.text: And the eyes of both of them were opened, and they knew that they were naked; so they sewed together fig leaves and made coverings for themselves.
The rip of leaves, close, then silence.

events.speaker: GUIDE
events.text: This is the only window the narrator gives into her mind, and it climbs. Good for food: the appetite. Pleasing to the eyes: the eye. Desirable for wisdom: ambition.

events.speaker: GUIDE
events.text: Desirable is the verb of the tenth commandment.

events.speaker: READER
events.text: You shall not covet

events.speaker: GUIDE
events.text: What God made to be enjoyed becomes something to be seized. And the man was with her the whole time, saying nothing at all.

events.speaker: GUIDE
events.text: Their eyes are opened, as the serpent promised. But what they see is their own exposure. One act fractures every relationship at once. They hide from God, they cover themselves from each other, and the fig leaves are their own attempt to fix it.

Set piece: the voice in the garden. Evening. A wind enters the garden from far off and moves through it in one long wave, treetop after treetop bending, light shifting across the ground between the trunks, as though something walks there. No figure anywhere. The man and the woman, in fig leaves, pressing back among dark trunks.

events.speaker: READER
events.text: Then the man and his wife heard the voice of the LORD God walking in the garden in the breeze of the day, and they hid themselves from the presence of the LORD God among the trees of the garden.

Set piece: the voice in the garden, no narration. Wind like footsteps, each wave nearer and louder; the score builds under it to an immense held chord; the pair's breathing, close; then everything stops.

events.speaker: READER
events.text: But the LORD God called out to the man,

events.speaker: GOD
events.text: “Where are you?”
Silence. Hold on the trees.

events.speaker: READER
events.text: “I heard Your voice in the garden,” he replied, “and I was afraid because I was naked; so I hid myself.”

The wilderness camp at dusk: the tent sanctuary at the centre, smoke rising from before its gate, a wind moving through the camp and stirring the tent cloths. The brick-maker stands at his door and listens.

events.speaker: GUIDE
events.text: Walking is the very word Israel would later use for God's presence moving through their camp. Their sanctuary was a garden like this one. And here, the man and the woman hide from Him among the trees He planted.

events.speaker: GUIDE
events.text: Many readers see this question as the centre of the whole chapter. The turning point is not the eating. It is the God who comes looking. He knows where they are. He asks so that the guilty will speak the truth, as He later asks Cain,

events.speaker: READER
events.text: Where is your brother Abel?

events.speaker: GUIDE
events.text: and Elijah,

events.speaker: READER
events.text: What are you doing here?

events.speaker: GUIDE
events.text: God's first word to fallen humanity is not a sentence. It is a search.

events.chapter: The woman whom You gave me
events.text: Failing light. The man in fig leaves among dark trunks, chest up, head lowered, not meeting the light; then the woman, the same; the serpent lying still in the grass between them.

events.chapter: The woman whom You gave me
events.speaker: GOD
events.text: “Who told you that you were naked?”

events.chapter: The woman whom You gave me
events.speaker: READER
events.text: asked the LORD God.

events.chapter: The woman whom You gave me
events.speaker: GOD
events.text: “Have you eaten from the tree of which I commanded you not to eat?”

events.chapter: The woman whom You gave me
events.speaker: READER
events.text: And the man answered, “The woman whom You gave me, she gave me fruit from the tree, and I ate it.”

events.chapter: The woman whom You gave me
events.speaker: READER
events.text: Then the LORD God said to the woman,

events.chapter: The woman whom You gave me
events.speaker: GOD
events.text: “What is this you have done?”

events.chapter: The woman whom You gave me
events.speaker: READER
events.text: “The serpent deceived me,” she replied, “and I ate.”

events.chapter: The woman whom You gave me
events.text: Graphic over a slow push across the garden floor: three marks, the serpent, the woman, the man. A line draws the sin down from serpent to woman to man; the questions climb back from man to woman; the blame slides back down to the serpent; then the sentences run the first way again, serpent, woman, man.

events.chapter: The woman whom You gave me
events.speaker: GUIDE
events.text: Look at the shape of it. The sin travels from serpent to woman to man. God's questions run the other way, man then woman, and the blame is passed back down the line. The sentences will retrace the first order.

events.chapter: The woman whom You gave me
events.speaker: GUIDE
events.text: The man said nothing until he was questioned, and now he speaks to excuse himself. The woman whom You gave me. What she says is true, but it is not a defence.

events.chapter: The woman whom You gave me
events.speaker: GUIDE
events.text: And God puts no question to the serpent. He does not negotiate with evil. He sentences it.
Bare dust at the garden's edge in low light: the serpent going on its belly through the dust, its trail a long line behind it, the wind blowing dust across it.

events.speaker: READER
events.text: So the LORD God said to the serpent:

events.speaker: GOD
events.text: “Because you have done this, cursed are you above all livestock and every beast of the field! On your belly will you go, and dust you will eat, all the days of your life.

events.speaker: GUIDE
events.text: Cursed falls on the serpent and on the ground, never on the man or the woman themselves. And even in Isaiah's renewed world, this one sentence still stands:

events.speaker: READER
events.text: the food of the serpent will be dust
Dawn breaking low over the dust; a single line of gold light falling across the ground. The serpent rears in shadow at the edge of the light.

events.speaker: GOD
events.text: And I will put enmity between you and the woman, and between your seed and her seed. He will crush your head, and you will strike his heel.”
One low boom, then silence.

events.speaker: GUIDE
events.text: Enmity means open war. The rescue of the world begins as God's own declaration of war on evil.

events.speaker: GUIDE
events.text: One verb stands behind both blows, the head and the heel. The difference is the target: a fatal blow against a wounding one. And the seed is he. Even the old Greek translators heard a person in this promise. A long war between two lines, but the decisive blow is struck by one.

events.speaker: GUIDE
events.text: This is the first announcement of the gospel, and it is spoken before a single sentence falls on the man and the woman.

Montage: the long war, fast and dark, two to three seconds a shot. Two offerings smoking on two altars in a field, one smoke rising, one blown flat; a staff lying in a field at dusk; a line of graves along a hillside, one after another; a great brick tower rising on a plain and people walking east toward it; a long column of captives walking east across a desert under guard toward a great walled city. The words AND THEN HE DIED appear again and again on screen, faster each time. Last: the serpent rearing to strike in the dust. Cut to black.
Montage: the long war, no narration. Driving low percussion; a hit on every AND THEN HE DIED; it stops dead on the strike.
The garden under a heavy sky at dusk, wind bending the long grass; the woman, in fig leaves, chest up, her face to the wind.

events.speaker: READER
events.text: To the woman He said:

events.speaker: GOD
events.text: “I will sharply increase your pain in childbirth; in pain you will bring forth children. Your desire will be for your husband, and he will rule over you.”

events.speaker: GUIDE
events.text: Her pain is the same word as the man's toil: the sentence falls on both in the same currency. And the desire and the rule describe a marriage bent by sin, not God's design. It is a sorrowful description of the world under judgment, never a charter for it.

Beyond the trees, a hard field under a hot sky: thorns and thistles bursting up through cracked ground in time lapse; the man's hands, bleeding, tearing at the thorns; sweat running down his brow, his face from the chest up.

events.speaker: READER
events.text: And to Adam He said:

events.speaker: GOD
events.text: “Because you have listened to the voice of your wife and have eaten from the tree of which I commanded you not to eat, cursed is the ground because of you; through toil you will eat of it all the days of your life.

events.speaker: GOD
events.text: Both thorns and thistles it will yield for you, and you will eat the plants of the field.

events.speaker: GOD
events.text: By the sweat of your brow you will eat your bread, until you return to the ground, because out of it were you taken. For dust you are, and to dust you shall return.”

Set piece: dust to dust. The opening of The Garden played backward: the man's eye closing; his face going still; the earth taking him back, the dust drawing in where he lay; a single grain of dust in macro; then the camera rising from the grain, fast, up over bare ground, up through the clouds, up into the high cold light above the world, and holding there.

Set piece: dust to dust, no narration. The breath from The Garden, played in reverse, drawn back out; the score from The Garden's opening, slowed and darkened; wind rush rising with the camera; silence at the top.

events.speaker: GUIDE
events.text: Chapter two ran from dust to a living man. Chapter three runs that film backward. The man taken from the ground will return to it. And from here a refrain tolls through Genesis, beginning with Adam himself:

events.speaker: READER
events.text: and then he died
Silence.

events.speaker: GUIDE
events.text: Yet mercy is laced through the judgment. Childbearing goes on, so the promised seed can still come. Work goes on, so life goes on. Judgment is real, but it is bounded.
First light over the garden after the night. The man and the woman standing together among the trees, chest up, in fig leaves, his face toward her.

events.speaker: READER
events.text: And Adam named his wife Eve, because she would be the mother of all the living.

events.speaker: GUIDE
events.text: Eve sounds like the Hebrew for living. In the very hour death enters, he names her the mother of all the living. A small act of hope in God's promise.
Close: simple garments of skin laid over two pairs of shoulders in warm light; the fig leaves falling to the ground. No hands from above, no figure.

events.speaker: READER
events.text: And the LORD God made garments of skin for Adam and his wife, and He clothed them.

The tabernacle courtyard by day, seen from across the camp: men in new white linen tunics standing in a line before the bronze altar, an older man in a plain robe fastening a sash on the first of them, faces small and far off. The brick-maker watching from the crowd at the courtyard gate.

events.speaker: GUIDE
events.text: The fig leaves were their own covering. These garments are God's. And the words are the ones used when Moses clothed Israel's priests. The brick-maker would have watched it happen: tunics, the same word, put on by another's hands.

events.speaker: GUIDE
events.text: The text does not describe a sacrifice, so the link is an inference, but a fair one. The covering came from a life taken.
The tree of life at the far centre of the garden in soft light, seen from a great distance through the trees, wind in its leaves; no figure.

events.speaker: READER
events.text: Then the LORD God said,

events.speaker: GOD
events.text: “Behold, the man has become like one of Us, knowing good and evil. And now, lest he reach out his hand and take also from the tree of life, and eat, and live forever...”

events.speaker: GUIDE
events.text: Even the exile is a mercy. It guards them from living forever in a fallen state.

Set piece: east of Eden. The man and the woman, clothed in skins, walking east out of the garden at dusk, seen from behind, the trees ending, a wide dry land opening before them. Behind them, in the eastern opening between the great trees, fire: a whirling sword of flame, a long blade of living fire turning in the air, its light flashing on the trunks; around it, vast shapes of wings made of flame and shadow, never faces, never figures. The camera pulls back and up until they are two specks in the dark land and the flame is a single point of fire behind them.

events.speaker: READER
events.text: Therefore the LORD God banished him from the Garden of Eden to work the ground from which he had been taken.

events.speaker: READER
events.text: So He drove out the man and stationed cherubim on the east side of the Garden of Eden, along with a whirling sword of flame to guard the way to the tree of life.

Set piece: east of Eden, no narration. The sword ignites with a roar; the biggest swell in the film, choir and drums; the fire turning; their footsteps on hard ground; the pull back; the music drains away to wind and one far crackle of flame.

events.speaker: GUIDE
events.text: Stationed is the verb of God's dwelling, the root of the word for the tabernacle. The guard that keeps sinners out is described in the language of God's house.

The wilderness camp: the tabernacle gate, facing east; then inside the holy place in low lamplight, the great veil, blue, purple and scarlet, with cherubim woven into it. The brick-maker outside the courtyard gate, at dusk, looking in but never going in.

events.speaker: GUIDE
events.text: To Israel this sounded like being barred from the sanctuary. Its door faced east, and cherubim were woven into the veil before the Most Holy Place. No one simply walked back in.

events.speaker: GUIDE
events.text: And Israel heard its own story in Adam. Given a good land and one word to keep, warned of death, they disobeyed, and they too were carried east, into exile in Babylon. Hosea says they

events.speaker: READER
events.text: like Adam, have transgressed the covenant

events.speaker: GUIDE
events.text: East becomes a direction in Genesis. Cain settles east of Eden. The builders of Babel journey east. Humanity keeps moving away from the presence it lost.
A wilderness of stone and dry hills at first light, empty; loose stones on the ground, each one shaped like a loaf; heat shimmer. No figures.
Wind over the empty wilderness; a new cue begins, low and patient.

events.speaker: GUIDE
events.text: Verse fifteen never names the victor, and the rest of the Bible keeps watching for him. The promise narrows to Abraham, then to David, and comes to rest on one person. God sent His Son, Paul says,

events.speaker: READER
events.text: born of a woman

events.speaker: GUIDE
events.text: Luke traces Jesus back to

events.speaker: READER
events.text: the son of Adam, the son of God

events.speaker: GUIDE
events.text: and the very next scene is the temptation. The last Adam meets the same enemy, in a wilderness instead of a garden, hungry instead of surrounded by fruit. The serpent began by questioning what God said. Jesus answers with what God said:

events.speaker: READER
events.text: It is written
One sustained tone over the stones.
An olive grove at night across a dry stream bed, torchlight moving between the trees; a crown of thorns lying on a flat stone; a rough wooden beam against a dark sky; no figures.

events.speaker: GUIDE
events.text: Adam hid among the trees. Christ was hung on a tree. Adam reached for what was forbidden. Christ, in a garden, prayed,

events.speaker: READER
events.text: not as I will, but as You will

events.speaker: GUIDE
events.text: Adam wore thorns as the fruit of his sin. Christ wore them as a crown. Adam left the garden to die. Christ was laid in a garden tomb, and rose. The promise never pictured a victory without cost. He shared our flesh and blood,

events.speaker: READER
events.text: so that by His death He might destroy him who holds the power of death

events.speaker: GUIDE
events.text: The strike to the heel and the crushing of the head happen in the same act.

Set piece: the veil to the empty tomb. Darkness over the land; the ground shakes; in the holy place the great veil with its cherubim tears from top to bottom and light floods through the tear; dawn in a garden, a rock cut tomb, the stone rolled back, light on the path; at the foot of the rock, in the dust, the serpent lies still, and the wind blows it away as dust. No figures.

Set piece: the veil to the empty tomb, no narration. Silence and darkness; a deep rumble; the tear, loud, cloth ripping from top to bottom; the score bursts into light; birdsong at the tomb; the same wind that walked in the garden.

The torn veil from inside, light pouring through it; then a radiant city with a river of clear water running through its centre and the tree of life on both banks, fruit in the light. No flame, no guard: the way open.

events.speaker: GUIDE
events.text: The cherubim that barred the way to life stood again over the mercy seat in Israel's sanctuary, where God promised,

events.speaker: READER
events.text: I will meet with you there

events.speaker: GUIDE
events.text: The guard at the door of Eden became the throne of atonement. And when Jesus died, the veil with its cherubim was torn from top to bottom. Believers now come in

events.speaker: READER
events.text: by the new and living way opened for us through the curtain of His body

events.speaker: GUIDE
events.text: The Bible closes by undoing this chapter. No longer any curse. The tree of life open beside the river. And the pair who hid from God among the trees are answered by a people who

events.speaker: READER
events.text: will see His face
The city and the tree of life, the river in the light. The warmest swell in the film, no narration.
Dawn in the wilderness camp. The brick-maker steps out of his dark tent into first light and walks toward the tabernacle gate, the smoke rising before it.

events.speaker: GUIDE
events.text: So hear God's questions as grace. The right answer to His question is not to hide and not to blame. It is to come out, confess, and trust the God who promised a Rescuer and clothed the naked.

events.speaker: GUIDE
events.text: God covered their shame with garments He provided. What are you using to cover your own shame, and what would it mean to receive God's covering in Christ instead?
Hold on the light.
East of Eden at evening: a field of hard ground, two smokes rising from two altars, and between them a young man looking back over his shoulder at a door in the dusk. Cut to black.

events.speaker: GUIDE
events.text: East of Eden, the first children are born. Two brothers bring offerings to God. And the next time God comes asking a question, it will be about a brother.
